title: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
summary: How Linux decides who may do what, and where attacks land and get caught: files, accounts, permission bits, setuid, sudo, processes, services, SSH, updates and logs, with five real cases.
outcomes: Explain how the kernel picks the owner, group or others permission triplet and compute modes with octal and umask
Explain why setuid programs are high-value targets, using PwnKit and Dirty COW as examples
Read sudoers rules, sudo and sshd log lines, and spot failed-then-accepted login sequences
Read a process tree and recognise suspicious parentage, as in Shellshock
Harden SSH with keys and sshd_config, and explain the regreSSHion race and the xz-utils supply chain backdoor
List the Linux persistence locations an intruder uses and the defender check for each

lessons.title: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view

blocks.md:
Linux keeps everything in one tree of directories that starts at `/`, called the root directory. Configuration, logs, programs, devices and even live information about running programs all appear as files somewhere in that tree.

That is good news for a defender. If you know which directory holds what, you know where secrets sit, where anyone can write, and where evidence of an attack lands. Start by listing the top of the tree on any Linux machine:

blocks.code:
ls /
bin   dev  home  lib64  mnt  proc  run   srv  tmp  var
boot  etc  lib   media  opt  root  sbin  sys  usr
blocks.caption: The command, then its output on a typical Debian or Ubuntu server. Each name is a directory with a defined job.

blocks.md:
The layout follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), a shared convention that distributions follow so tools know where to look. The Linux manual page `hier(7)` describes the directories that matter most here:

- `/etc` holds configuration files local to this machine: user accounts, the SSH server settings, scheduled jobs.
- `/home` holds each user's home directory; `/root` is the home of the root (administrator) account.
- `/tmp` holds temporary files that may be deleted without notice, for example at boot.
- `/var` holds variable data that changes while the system runs; `/var/log` holds log files.
- `/proc` is the mount point of the proc filesystem, which gives information about running processes and the kernel.
- `/usr/bin` holds most programs users run; `/dev` holds device files; `/boot` holds the kernel and boot loader files.

blocks.title: The tree, coloured by what a defender cares about

scenes.caption: The top of the tree. Every path on the system starts at / and goes down through one of these directories.
Secrets and trust settings: /etc holds account and service configuration, /root and /home hold users' private files such as SSH keys.
Shared scratch space: every user can create files in /tmp, so it is a common place for dropped tools. It is wiped at boot on many systems.
Evidence: /var/log keeps history on disk, and /proc shows what is running right now, including the command line and executable of every process.
Programs: /usr/bin and /boot hold the code the system trusts. A changed file here is serious, which is why packages record checksums for them (lesson 8).

blocks.md:
`/proc` deserves a closer look because it is the defender's live view. It is a pseudo-filesystem: nothing in it is stored on disk; the kernel (the core of the operating system that controls hardware, memory and every process) generates each file when you read it. Each running process gets a directory named after its process ID number, for example `/proc/1234/`, containing:

- `cmdline`: the full command line the process was started with.
- `exe`: a link to the program file it is running.
- `environ`: its environment variables (named text settings such as `PATH` or `HOME` that a program inherits from the process that started it).
- `status`: its user IDs, memory use and state.

The word `self` is a shortcut for whichever process is reading, so `/proc/self/` describes your own command.

blocks.code:
ls -l /proc/self/exe
lrwxrwxrwx 1 alice alice 0 Nov 13 09:12 /proc/self/exe -> /usr/bin/ls

tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/1/cmdline; echo
/sbin/init splash

grep -E '^(Name|Uid|PPid)' /proc/self/status
Name:   grep
PPid:   2231
Uid:    1000    1000    1000    1000
blocks.caption: Reading /proc. cmdline separates arguments with zero bytes, so tr turns them into spaces. The four Uid numbers are the real, effective, saved and filesystem user IDs; lesson 4 explains the first two, which are the ones that matter here.

blocks.md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

Learn the map once: configuration in `/etc`, user secrets in `/home` and `/root`, shared scratch in `/tmp`, history in `/var/log`, the live view in `/proc`. Almost every later lesson points at one of these places.

blocks.question: On a server you find a process whose /proc/<pid>/exe link reads /tmp/.cache/kworker (deleted). What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Normal: kernel worker threads always run from /tmp
Suspicious: a program was started from a world-writable directory and its file was then removed
Harmless: (deleted) only means the process has exited
Proof that the disk is failing
blocks.explain: Kernel threads have no executable file at all, and a process that has exited has no /proc directory. A running program whose file lived in /tmp and was deleted after starting is a common way to leave fewer traces on disk, so it deserves investigation.

blocks.question: Which directory would you expect to hold the SSH server's configuration file?
options: /var/log
/proc
/etc
/usr/bin
blocks.explain: Configuration local to the machine lives under /etc (the SSH server reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config). /var/log holds logs, /proc is generated live by the kernel, and /usr/bin holds programs.

blocks.md: Every process on Linux runs as some user, and the kernel decides what it may touch by number, not by name. A **UID** (user identifier) is the number for a user; a **GID** (group identifier) is the number for a group, a named set of users who share access to files. The command `id` shows yours:

blocks.code:
id
uid=1000(alice) gid=1000(alice) groups=1000(alice),10(wheel)

grep '^alice:' /etc/passwd
alice:x:1000:1000:Alice Example:/home/alice:/bin/bash

getent group wheel
wheel:x:10:alice
blocks.caption: Each command followed by its output. Names in brackets are only labels for the numbers; the kernel compares the numbers. wheel is a traditional name for the administrators group that may use sudo (lesson 5).

blocks.md: `/etc/passwd` is the account list. Each line has seven fields separated by colons. Despite its name it no longer holds passwords: the file must be readable by everyone, because programs such as `ls` need it to turn UID 1000 back into the name alice. Long ago the password hash sat here too, and anyone could copy it and try to crack it offline, so modern systems put an `x` in that field and move the hash to a separate file, `/etc/shadow`, that only root can read (`passwd(5)`).

blocks.title: One line of /etc/passwd, field by field

scenes.caption: The line alice:x:1000:1000:Alice Example:/home/alice:/bin/bash split at its colons into seven fields.
Name and password field. The x means the real password hash lives in /etc/shadow.
UID and primary GID. These numbers, not the name, are what file ownership and permission checks use. UID 0 is root.
GECOS (a free-text comment, usually the full name), the home directory, and the program started at login. Service accounts often get /usr/sbin/nologin here.
What an intruder might change: a second account with UID 0, or a login shell on a service account that should have none.

blocks.md:
GECOS is a historical name: the passwd manual explains it stands for General Electric Comprehensive Operating System (renamed GCOS when GE sold that division to Honeywell), and quotes Dennis Ritchie, co-creator of Unix, recalling that they sent printer output and batch jobs to a GCOS machine and used this field to store the identification details those jobs needed.

**Root** is the account with UID 0, the superuser. The kernel skips ordinary file permission checks for it. What makes an account root is the number 0, not the name: a line `backup:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash` creates a second root account under a harmless-sounding name.

`/etc/shadow` has nine colon-separated fields (`shadow(5)`): login name, password hash, date of last change (in days since 1 January 1970), minimum and maximum password age, warning period, inactivity period, account expiry date and a reserved field. Special values in the hash field matter during an investigation:

- An empty field means the account can log in with no password at all.
- A field starting with `!` means the password is locked.
- A value like `*` or `!` that is not a valid hash means no password login is possible, though other methods such as SSH keys may still work.

scenes.caption: alice's shadow entry. The hash is shortened here; a real yescrypt hash is about 70 characters long.
Last change 20400 days after 1970-01-01, which is 2025-11-08. Minimum age 0 days, maximum 99999 (effectively never), warn 7 days before expiry.
Empty inactivity, expiry and reserved fields: no grace period, the account never expires.
An administrator ran passwd -l alice: the hash now starts with !, so password login is locked while the old hash is kept for unlocking.

blocks.md: The password field holds a **hash**: the output of a one-way function that is cheap to compute from the password but infeasible to reverse. At login the system hashes what you typed and compares. Each hash also includes a **salt**, a random value stored next to it, so two users with the same password get different hashes. The text before the salt names the algorithm: the `crypt(5)` manual lists prefix y for yescrypt (recommended for new hashes) and prefix 6 for SHA-512 crypt. Reading `/etc/shadow` gives an attacker material for offline guessing, which is why its permissions matter so much.

blocks.code:
# accounts with UID 0 (should be exactly one: root)
grep -E '^[^:]*:[^:]*:0:' /etc/passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash

# accounts whose password field is empty (should be none)
# sudo runs one command as root; lesson 5 explains it
sudo grep -E '^[^:]*::' /etc/shadow
blocks.caption: Two quick audits. The first prints every line whose third field (UID) is 0; the second prints shadow lines whose second field (the hash) is empty, meaning no password is needed.

blocks.prompt: You audit a server and see this line in /etc/passwd: `support:x:0:0:Support:/home/support:/bin/bash`. The account is called support, not root. Should you worry?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The UID field is 0, so any process running as support is root as far as the kernel is concerned: it bypasses file permissions and can read `/etc/shadow`, load kernel modules or add more accounts. Adding a UID 0 account is a known persistence trick (MITRE ATT&CK lists account creation as technique T1136.001). Check when it was added, who added it, and remove it.

blocks.md: Setting a user's shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin` or putting `*` in their password field does not fully disable them. The passwd manual notes such users may still run jobs through cron or log in by other means, and an SSH key in their home directory still works if the shell allows it. To retire an account, lock it, expire it and remove its keys.

blocks.question: Why is /etc/passwd readable by every user while /etc/shadow is readable only by root?
options: Programs everywhere need to map UIDs to names, but password hashes can be guessed offline if copied
Because /etc/passwd is encrypted and /etc/shadow is not
It is a historical accident with no security effect
So that users can change other users' passwords
blocks.explain: Name and UID lookups happen constantly, so passwd must be public. A copied hash can be attacked with unlimited offline guesses, so hashes were moved to shadow, which is unreadable to ordinary users.

blocks.question: A shadow entry's password field is completely empty. What does that mean?
options: The account is locked
The account can log in without a password, unless the login program blocks empty passwords
The password is stored in /etc/passwd instead
The account has expired
blocks.explain: shadow(5): an empty password field means the user can log in without a password, although some programs refuse empty passwords (for example sshd with PermitEmptyPasswords no, its default). A locked account has a field starting with !.

lessons.title: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check

blocks.md: Every file and directory has an owner (a UID), a group (a GID) and nine permission bits. The bits answer three questions (may I **r**ead, **w**rite, e**x**ecute?) for three classes of user: the owner, members of the file's group, and everyone else ("others"). `ls -l` shows them as a ten-character string:

blocks.code:
ls -l /etc/passwd report.txt deploy.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 root  root  1843 Nov  2 10:40 /etc/passwd
-rw-r----- 1 alice staff  512 Nov 13 09:05 report.txt
-rwxr-x--- 1 alice staff  210 Nov 13 09:07 deploy.sh
blocks.caption: The first character is the type (- file, d directory, l link). Then three triplets: owner, group, others. A dash means the bit is off.

blocks.md: Each triplet is three bits, so it fits in one **octal** digit (base 8, digits 0 to 7). Read is worth 4, write 2 and execute 1; add the ones that are on. `rwxr-x---` is 7, 5, 0, written `750`. This is why commands like `chmod 640 report.txt` use three digits: one per class.

blocks.title: From rwx letters to an octal mode

scenes.caption: deploy.sh has mode rwxr-x---. Each position has a fixed value: 4 for r, 2 for w, 1 for x.
Owner triplet: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.
Group triplet: 4 + 0 + 1 = 5. The group may read and run the script but not change it.
Others: 0. Together the mode is 750.
chmod 640 report.txt sets rw- r-- ---: the owner reads and writes, the group only reads, others get nothing.

blocks.md:
How does the kernel use these bits? The `path_resolution(7)` manual states the rule exactly. When a process opens a file:

1. If the process's user ID equals the file's owner, the **owner** triplet is used.
2. Otherwise, if the file's group is the process's group or one of its supplementary groups, the **group** triplet is used.
3. Otherwise the **others** triplet is used.

Only one triplet is ever consulted; the classes are not added together. Root is the exception: Linux divides root's powers into separate **capabilities**, and one called `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` skips these checks (DAC means discretionary access control, "discretionary" because the file's owner decides who gets in). Even root can execute a file only if at least one execute bit is set.

blocks.title: The kernel's permission check, simplified

scenes.caption: Alice (UID 1000, groups alice and staff) reads report.txt: owner alice, group staff, mode 640.
Alice owns the file, so the owner triplet rw- is chosen. Read is in it: allowed.
Bob (UID 1001) is in group staff and tries to write. Not the owner, but in the group, so the group triplet r-- is chosen. Write is missing: denied.
Carol (UID 1002) is in neither. Others triplet ---: denied.
Root reads it: the capability check comes first and permission bits are skipped.

blocks.prompt: Alice owns secret.txt and sets its mode to 077 (owner ---, group rwx, others rwx). Alice then runs `cat secret.txt`. What happens?
blocks.reveal: Permission denied. Alice is the owner, so the kernel uses the owner triplet `---` and stops there; it never looks at the generous group or others bits. (Alice can still `chmod` the file back, because changing the mode is a right of ownership, not a permission bit.) The lesson: classes are checked in order and only the first match counts.

blocks.md: For a **directory** the same letters mean different things. `r` lets you list the names inside; `x` (called search permission) lets you enter it and reach files by name; `w` together with `x` lets you create, delete and rename entries. That last point surprises people: write permission on a directory lets you delete files in it that you do not own, even files you cannot read. The sticky bit in the next lesson exists to fix exactly that.

New files do not start with mode 777. A program asks for a mode when it creates a file (usually 666 for files and 777 for directories), and the kernel clears whatever bits are set in the process's **umask** (the file mode creation mask, `umask(2)`). The typical default umask is 022, which removes write permission for group and others:

blocks.caption: The requested mode AND the inverse of the umask. With umask 077 the results are 0600 and 0700: nobody but the owner gets anything.

blocks.code:
umask
0022
touch notes.txt && mkdir drafts && ls -ld notes.txt drafts
drwxr-xr-x 2 alice alice 4096 Nov 13 09:20 drafts
-rw-r--r-- 1 alice alice    0 Nov 13 09:20 notes.txt

chmod 600 notes.txt          # owner read/write only
chown root:adm app.log       # change owner and group (root only)
chmod g+w,o-r app.log        # symbolic form: add group write, remove others read
blocks.caption: Commands with their output, then the tools that change modes and ownership. Only root may give a file to another owner.

blocks.md: `chmod 777` is not a fix for "permission denied". It lets every account on the machine, including a compromised web server account, modify the file. If a script run by root is world-writable, any user can make root run their code. Find the account that actually needs access and grant only that.
Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

blocks.question: app.log has owner root, group adm and mode 640. Bob is a member of adm. Can Bob read it? Can Bob append to it?
options: Neither
Both, because Bob is in the group
Append yes, read no
Read yes, append no
blocks.explain: Bob is not the owner but is in group adm, so the group triplet r-- applies: 4 means read only. Writing (including appending) needs the w bit, which only the owner has.

blocks.question: A service runs with umask 027 and creates a file, asking for mode 666. What mode does the file get?
blocks.explain: 666 AND NOT 027: the owner digit keeps 6, the group digit 6 loses write (2) to become 4, and the others digit 6 loses everything (7) to become 0. Result 640.

lessons.title: Setuid, setgid and sticky: borrowed privilege and its bugs

blocks.md:
A puzzle: ordinary users can change their own password with the `passwd` command, yet the new hash must be written into `/etc/shadow`, which only root can write. How?

The answer is three extra mode bits above the nine you know. The most important is **setuid** (set user ID on execution): when a program file with this bit is executed, the new process runs with the file owner's identity instead of the caller's. `passwd` is owned by root and has the bit set, so for as long as it runs, it acts as root.

blocks.code:
ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 68248 Mar 23  2025 /usr/bin/passwd

ls -ld /tmp
drwxrwxrwt 18 root root 4096 Nov 13 09:30 /tmp

stat -c '%a %n' /usr/bin/passwd /tmp
4755 /usr/bin/passwd
1777 /tmp
blocks.caption: The s in the owner's execute slot marks setuid; the t in the others' execute slot marks the sticky bit. stat prints the full octal mode, with the special bits as a fourth leading digit.

blocks.md: To see how this works you need the idea of real and effective IDs (`credentials(7)`). Every process carries a **real UID** (who started it) and an **effective UID** (whose permissions it uses right now). Normally they are equal. When a setuid program is started through the `execve` system call (the request to the kernel that replaces a process's program with a new one), the kernel sets the effective UID to the file's owner and leaves the real UID alone (`execve(2)`). The program can then see who really called it and decide what to allow: `passwd` lets alice change only alice's password.

blocks.title: What execve does with a setuid-root program

scenes.caption: Alice's shell runs with real and effective UID 1000. It cannot write /etc/shadow (mode 640, owner root).
Alice runs passwd. The file is owned by root and has mode 4755: the 4 is the setuid bit.
execve sees the setuid bit and starts the new program with effective UID 0. The real UID stays 1000, so passwd knows the caller is alice.
The permission check uses the effective UID, which is 0, so the write to /etc/shadow is allowed. passwd itself restricts alice to alice's own entry.
The risk: any bug in a setuid-root program runs with root's power, and its inputs (arguments, environment) come from the untrusted caller.

blocks.md:
The three special bits, from `inode(7)`:

- **setuid** (octal 4000, shown as `s` in the owner's execute slot): run as the file's owner.
- **setgid** (2000, `s` in the group slot): on a program, run with the file's group. On a directory, new files inherit the directory's group, which is handy for shared project folders.
- **sticky** (1000, `t` in the others slot): on a directory, a file inside can be renamed or deleted only by its owner, the directory's owner or root.

A capital `S` or `T` means the special bit is set but the matching execute bit is not. `/tmp` is mode 1777 (systemd creates it that way): everyone may create files there, and the sticky bit stops users from deleting or replacing each other's files.

Because setuid programs are such valuable targets, the system defends them. The dynamic linker, the part of the system that loads shared libraries when a program starts, runs setuid programs in "secure-execution mode" and ignores or strips dangerous environment variables such as `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (where to look for libraries) and `GCONV_PATH` that would otherwise let the caller load their own code (`ld.so(8)`). A filesystem mounted with the `nosuid` option ignores the bits completely. Defenders keep a list of setuid files and alert on new ones:

blocks.code:
# every setuid or setgid file on the root filesystem (-xdev: repeat per mount)
sudo find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -exec ls -l {} +

# keep a baseline and compare tomorrow
sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 | sort | sudo tee /root/suid-baseline.txt > /dev/null

# file capabilities: single root powers attached to a program, no setuid bit needed
sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
blocks.caption: The setuid search, a saved baseline, and getcap, which lists programs carrying file capabilities (for example cap_net_raw on ping). A new capability on an interpreter is as serious as a new setuid file.

blocks.md:
**Case: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034).** CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is the public catalogue that gives each known bug an ID. On 25 January 2022 the research team of Qualys, a security company, disclosed a bug in `pkexec`, a setuid-root program from polkit that lets a user run a command as another user if the policy allows it (formerly PolicyKit, a service that decides which unprivileged programs may perform privileged actions). It was installed by default on every major distribution and had been vulnerable since it was written in May 2009.

The bug: `pkexec` assumed it was always given at least one argument. A program's arguments (`argv`) and environment (`envp`) sit next to each other in memory. If a caller started pkexec with an empty argument list, its loop read `argv[1]`, which is past the end of the list and is really the first environment string, and later wrote a value back into it. That let a local user re-insert an environment variable the dynamic linker had just removed, and get their own library loaded as root.

blocks.title: PwnKit: reading one slot past the end of argv

scenes.caption: Normal call: pkexec ls. argv holds the program name and one argument, then the NULL that ends the list; envp follows directly after it.
Attack shape: started with zero arguments, so argc (the argument count) is 0 and argv[0] is already the terminating NULL.
The loop starts at n = 1 and reads argv[1]. There is no argv[1]: the slot belongs to envp[0], so pkexec treats an environment string as the program to run.
pkexec then writes the resolved path back into argv[1], overwriting envp[0]. That out-of-bounds write is how a stripped, dangerous variable gets back into the environment of a root process.
The fix: refuse to run when argc is less than 1, and never write into a slot that holds the list terminator.

blocks.caption: The fix works because it rejects the impossible case at the door (argc of 0) and also stops the write from landing outside argv.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Patch polkit. Until you can, Qualys recommended removing the setuid bit as a temporary mitigation, `chmod 0755 /usr/bin/pkexec`: without it the bug runs only with the caller's own privileges and gains nothing. The advisory notes that the published technique leaves messages in the system log, such as "The value for the SHELL variable was not found the /etc/shells file" (quoted as written), although it also warns that exploitation without log traces is possible. Detection therefore leans on version inventory, not only on logs.

**Case: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195).** Permission bits are enforced by the kernel, so a kernel bug can bypass all of them. Dirty COW was a race condition (a bug where the result depends on the timing of two concurrent operations) in the kernel's copy-on-write handling: the trick that lets processes share a read-only page of memory until one writes to it, and only then gives the writer a private copy (COW). Red Hat's advisory explains that an unprivileged local user could gain write access to read-only memory mappings and use it to modify setuid files. It affected kernels before 4.8.3 and was exploited in the wild: the disclosure FAQ credits Phil Oester with finding it, from an exploit seen in an HTTP packet capture. The disclosure FAQ adds that exploitation leaves nothing abnormal in the logs. The fix is a kernel update, and a kernel update takes effect only after a reboot.

"It is only a local bug" is a dangerous phrase. Local privilege escalation means any foothold, such as a hijacked web application running as `www-data`, becomes root. PwnKit and Dirty COW both needed only an ordinary account.

blocks.question: Why did `chmod 0755 /usr/bin/pkexec` work as a temporary PwnKit mitigation?
options: It made pkexec unreadable
Without the setuid bit, pkexec runs with the caller's own UID, so the bug yields no extra privilege
It blocked all environment variables
It moved pkexec out of PATH
blocks.explain: 4755 becomes 0755: the 4000 setuid bit is cleared. The memory bug still exists, but a process running as alice that misbehaves can only do what alice could already do.

blocks.question: In /tmp (mode 1777), user bob tries to delete /tmp/alice-upload.zip, which alice owns. What happens?
options: It fails, because the sticky bit allows only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root to delete it
It works, because /tmp is writable by everyone
It works only if the file's mode allows bob to write
It fails, because /tmp is owned by root
blocks.explain: Write permission on a directory normally allows deleting any entry. The sticky bit (the 1 in 1777) narrows that to the file's owner, the directory's owner and privileged processes, so bob is refused.

lessons.title: sudo and sudoers: controlled, logged use of root

blocks.md:
Logging in as root all day is risky: every typo runs with full power and the logs cannot tell which human did what. Two tools let a normal user act as root when needed.

- `su` (run a command with a **s**ubstitute **u**ser and group ID, per `su(1)`) asks for the *target* account's password. Sharing root's password with every admin defeats accountability.
- `sudo` (su "do", as its project describes it) asks for *your own* password, checks a policy saying what you may run, and records an audit trail of each command. Bob Coggeshall and Cliff Spencer first wrote it around 1980 at the State University of New York at Buffalo.

blocks.code:
sudo -l
User alice may run the following commands on web1:
    (ALL) ALL

sudo systemctl restart nginx
[sudo] password for alice:
blocks.caption: sudo -l lists what the policy allows you. Here alice may run any command as any user, which is common for admins and broad for everyone else.

blocks.md:
The policy lives in `/etc/sudoers` and files in `/etc/sudoers.d/`. Each user specification reads: who, on which host, as whom, which commands. Examples from the `sudoers(5)` manual:

- `root ALL = (ALL) ALL`: root, on any host, as any user, may run anything.
- `%wheel ALL = (ALL) ALL`: the same for members of group wheel (a leading `%` means a group). Many distributions grant sudo to an admin group like this; the group's name varies.
- `ray rushmore = NOPASSWD: /bin/kill, /bin/ls, /usr/bin/lprm`: ray may run only these three programs on host rushmore, without typing a password.

Always edit with `visudo`, which locks the file and checks the syntax before saving, so a typo cannot lock every admin out.

blocks.title: One sudo command, from request to log line

scenes.caption: alice asks sudo to restart a service. sudo is itself a setuid-root program, so it starts with effective UID 0 but runs nothing yet.
sudo reads the policy: does any rule let alice run /usr/bin/systemctl as root on this host?
alice proves their identity with their own password, not root's.
Before running anything, sudo writes the audit line: who, which terminal, which directory, as whom, which command.
Only then does the command run as root. A denied request would be logged too, with a reason such as command not allowed.

blocks.code:
Nov 13 09:41:07 web1 sudo:    alice : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/alice ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
Nov 13 09:44:52 web1 sudo:      bob : command not allowed ; TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/bob ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/cat /etc/shadow
Nov 13 09:45:10 web1 sudo:    carol : user NOT in sudoers ; TTY=pts/2 ; PWD=/home/carol ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash
blocks.caption: What sudo writes, in the format the sudoers manual documents. TTY is the terminal the command came from; pts/0 is a pseudoterminal, the kind an SSH session uses. The second and third lines are denials, with the reason after the user name. Both deserve a look.

blocks.md: The danger in sudoers is granting more than you meant. A rule that allows one specific program can still be a full root grant if that program can start other programs. Text editors, pagers such as `less`, and many scripting tools can open a shell from inside, and that shell inherits root. The sudoers manual offers two defences: the `NOEXEC` tag, which stops many programs from starting others, and `sudoedit`, which lets a user edit a file as root while the editor itself runs as the user. Watch also for rules that allow a script the user can modify, or a wildcard that matches more arguments than intended.

blocks.code:
# risky: vim can run shell commands, so this is effectively root
alice  ALL = (root) /usr/bin/vim /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# safer: alice edits a copy as alice; sudoedit writes it back as root
alice  ALL = (root) sudoedit /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# risky: NOPASSWD on everything means a stolen session is instant root
%deploy ALL = (ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL

# narrower: one fixed command line; arguments must match exactly
%deploy ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp
blocks.caption: Rules side by side. The safer versions limit both which program runs as root and what that program can do.

blocks.md: `sudo -l` is also the first thing an intruder runs after landing on an account, because broad sudo rights are the shortest path to root. Run it yourself for each account and treat anything beyond a short, specific list as a finding.

blocks.question: A rule says `bob ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/less /var/log/syslog`. Why is this close to giving bob full root?
options: Because NOPASSWD rules are ignored
Because /var/log/syslog contains root's password
Because less can start a shell from inside, and that shell would run as root
It is not; bob can only read one file
blocks.explain: less, like many pagers and editors, can run a shell command from within. Since less runs as root under sudo, that shell is a root shell. Use a read-only alternative, NOEXEC, or give bob group read access to the log instead.

blocks.question: What is the main accountability advantage of sudo over sharing the root password for su?
options: sudo is faster
sudo encrypts commands
su cannot run single commands
Each person uses their own password and every command is logged under their name
blocks.explain: With su, many people know one secret and logs show only that root did something. sudo authenticates the individual and writes a line per command naming the real user, terminal and command.

lessons.title: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals

blocks.md:
A **process** is a running program: code plus its memory, open files and identity. Each has a **PID** (process ID), a unique number, and a **PPID** (parent process ID), the PID of the process that created it (`credentials(7)`).

New processes are made in two steps. `fork` creates a child that is a copy of the parent; `execve` then replaces the child's program with a new one (per `exec(3)`, the v means the arguments come as a vector, an array, and the e that an environment is passed too). Your shell does this for every command you type, so processes form a tree. The first process, PID 1, is started by the kernel at boot; on most current distributions it is systemd.

blocks.code:
ps -eo pid,ppid,user,cmd --forest
  PID  PPID USER     CMD
    1     0 root     /sbin/init splash
  612     1 root     sshd: /usr/sbin/sshd -D [listener]
 2207   612 root      \_ sshd: alice [priv]
 2229  2207 alice         \_ sshd: alice@pts/0
 2231  2229 alice             \_ -bash
 2290  2231 alice                 \_ ps -eo pid,ppid,user,cmd --forest
  880     1 root     /usr/sbin/apache2 -k start
 1501   880 www-data  \_ /usr/sbin/apache2 -k start
blocks.caption: ps with an ASCII-art tree (--forest). Read it as a family tree: the SSH login chain under sshd, and web server workers under apache2. Since OpenSSH 9.8 the per-login processes are named sshd-session instead of sshd.

blocks.md:
Defenders read process trees because **parentage reveals intent**. An interactive shell whose parent is the SSH server is a login. The same shell whose parent is a web server worker is almost never legitimate: web servers serve pages, they do not usually start `bash`. Many detection rules are exactly this: alert when a shell, a downloader or a network tool appears under a process that should not start one.

**Case: Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271).** The researcher Stephane Chazelas found that GNU Bash (the shell from GNU, the free software project whose name means GNU's Not Unix; Bash means the Bourne-Again SHell, named as a pun on Stephen Bourne, author of sh, the Seventh Edition Unix shell that is the direct ancestor of today's Unix shell) treated environment variables whose values looked like a function definition specially: at startup it imported the function and also ran any commands written after the function body. It was disclosed on 24 September 2014 and affected Bash through version 4.3.

Why that mattered: many programs pass untrusted data into environment variables before starting bash. Red Hat's advisory lists the routes. Web servers running CGI scripts (Common Gateway Interface, the old standard for a web server to run a program per request) put request headers into variables named `HTTP_...`; DHCP clients (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, which hands out network settings) run scripts with values from the network, typically as root; and SSH `ForceCommand` setups (which force every login to run one fixed command) meant to restrict users could be bypassed. The CGI script itself could be perfectly innocent; the bug fired as soon as bash started.

scenes.caption: Normal: apache2 workers serve requests. A request to a CGI script makes a worker start the script, here a bash script, as user www-data.
The server copies the request's headers into environment variables such as HTTP_USER_AGENT before starting bash. The attacker controls those values.
Vulnerable bash parses a value that starts like a function definition and runs the commands placed after it, before the script's first line.
What a defender sees: a downloader or shell whose ancestors are apache2. That parent-child pair is the alert, whatever the payload was.
Patched bash no longer runs code placed after a function definition in a variable, so the same request just runs the script.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# /usr/lib/cgi-bin/status.cgi : an innocent script
echo "Content-Type: text/plain"
echo
uptime

# Red Hat's 2014 self-test (only ever runs echo, safe on your own machine)
env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' bash -c "echo this is a test"
# vulnerable bash prints:   vulnerable
#                           this is a test
# patched bash prints:      this is a test   (2014 patches also printed warnings)
blocks.caption: The script has no bug; bash did. The self-test sets one variable shaped like a function with an extra echo after it and checks whether bash runs that echo.

blocks.md: **Defender view for Shellshock.** Prevent: update bash (the first patch was incomplete, and follow-up CVEs such as CVE-2014-7169 needed more updates), and avoid shell-based CGI. Detect: web server access logs showing header values beginning with `() {`, and process trees with shells or downloaders under the web server user. Respond: treat any host where that tree appeared as compromised.

**Signals** are small asynchronous notifications the kernel delivers to a process (`signal(7)`). Each has a name and, on common architectures such as x86 and ARM, a number:

- `SIGHUP` (1, hangup: the terminal went away). Many daemons (background service programs, next lesson) treat it as "reload your configuration".
- `SIGINT` (2, interrupt): what Ctrl-C sends.
- `SIGKILL` (9): ends the process immediately.
- `SIGTERM` (15, terminate): the polite request to exit; it is what `kill` sends by default.
- `SIGSTOP` (19 on x86): pauses the process.

A process may catch or ignore most signals, but `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. An unprivileged user may only signal their own processes (`kill(2)`), which is why a normal account cannot stop a root service.

blocks.code:
kill 4242            # SIGTERM: please exit (can be caught)
kill -HUP 612        # many daemons reload their config on SIGHUP
kill -STOP 4242      # freeze a suspicious process to inspect it
kill -9 4242         # SIGKILL: cannot be caught or ignored
blocks.caption: During incident response, SIGSTOP is useful: a frozen process keeps its memory and open files for investigation, where a kill would destroy them.

blocks.md: Read processes as a tree. Who started a process (its parent, its user, its command line in `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`) usually tells you more than its name, because names are trivial to fake.

blocks.question: Which observation is the strongest sign of compromise on a web server?
options: sshd running as root with PPID 1
bash running as www-data whose parent is an apache2 worker
A process named kworker
cron running as root
blocks.explain: sshd under PID 1 and cron as root are normal. Kernel threads are named kworker but have no executable. A shell spawned by a web server worker is the classic sign of command injection (untrusted input ending up in a shell command) or a Shellshock-style bug.

blocks.question: You want to stop a suspicious process but keep its memory for analysis. Which signal fits best?
options: SIGSTOP
SIGKILL
SIGTERM
SIGHUP
blocks.explain: SIGSTOP pauses the process and cannot be caught, so the program cannot react; its memory and file handles remain for inspection. SIGKILL and SIGTERM end it, and SIGHUP often just reloads configuration.

lessons.title: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in

blocks.md: Much of what runs on a server is not started by a person. A **daemon** is a program that runs in the background providing a service; names ending in d follow this habit, so `sshd` is the daemon of OpenSSH, the SSH implementation written by the OpenBSD project (developers of OpenBSD, a free Unix-like operating system) and shipped by almost every Linux distribution. On most distributions daemons are started and supervised by **systemd**, the system and service manager that runs as PID 1. Each service is described by a small text file called a unit.

blocks.code:
systemctl status ssh
* ssh.service - OpenBSD Secure Shell server
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Thu 2025-11-13 08:02:11 UTC; 1h 41min ago
   Main PID: 612 (sshd)
     CGroup: /system.slice/ssh.service
             `-612 "sshd: /usr/sbin/sshd -D [listener] 0 of 10-100 startups"

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled
blocks.caption: status shows where the unit file lives, whether it starts at boot (enabled) and its main PID. The last two commands list running services and services set to start at boot.

blocks.md:
A unit file says what to run, as whom, and when to start it. `systemd.unit(5)` defines where unit files are loaded from. Packages install theirs under `/usr/lib/systemd/system`; administrators put their own in `/etc/systemd/system`, and files there take precedence. Drop-in files in a `name.service.d/` directory can change single settings of an existing unit.

That precedence is useful for admins and attractive to intruders: a new file in `/etc/systemd/system`, or a drop-in that changes `ExecStart` of a trusted service, runs code at every boot as whatever user it names, often root. MITRE ATT&CK, a public knowledge base of observed attacker techniques run by the non-profit MITRE, lists this as T1543.002, Systemd Service.

blocks.title: Where systemd finds units, and where to look for changes

scenes.caption: At boot systemd (PID 1) reads unit files and starts the enabled ones. Packages ship units in /usr/lib/systemd/system.
Admin units in /etc/systemd/system take precedence over the packaged ones, and drop-in directories override single settings.
Persistence: an intruder adds evil.service in /etc/systemd/system, or a drop-in that swaps ExecStart of a trusted service. It now runs at every boot.
Timers are units too: a .timer file can start a service on a schedule, a modern replacement for cron (ATT&CK T1053.006).
Defender check: compare /etc/systemd/system and drop-ins against your baseline, and read every ExecStart line you did not write.

blocks.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/report.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly report generator

[Service]
User=report
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/report.sh
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=full
PrivateTmp=yes

[Install]
# start in the normal multi-user boot once enabled
WantedBy=multi-user.target
blocks.caption: A well-behaved unit. It runs as an unprivileged account; NoNewPrivileges blocks gaining privilege through setuid programs; ProtectSystem=full makes /usr, /boot and /etc read-only to it; PrivateTmp gives it its own /tmp. systemd-analyze security scores a unit's sandboxing.

blocks.md: **cron** is the older scheduler. The `cron` daemon checks its tables every minute and runs any command whose time matches (`crontab(5)`). A crontab line has five time fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and then the command. Each user has a personal crontab, edited with `crontab -e` and run as that user; system tables in `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d/` have an extra field naming the user to run as.

blocks.code:
# m   h  dom mon dow  command
  30  2  *   *   *    /usr/local/bin/backup.sh        # 02:30 every day
  */5 *  *   *   *    /usr/local/bin/healthcheck      # every 5 minutes
  0   4  *   *   sun  /usr/local/bin/rotate-keys      # 04:00 on Sundays

# /etc/cron.d/backup has a user field after the five time fields
  30  2  *   *   *    root  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh

crontab -l                 # your own table
sudo crontab -l -u www-data
ls -la /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.daily /etc/crontab
blocks.caption: A crontab, then the commands an investigator runs to read every table on the box.

blocks.md: A cron job run by root that executes a script writable by another user is a privilege escalation waiting to happen: whoever can edit the script chooses what root runs every night. When auditing, check the permissions of every file a root job calls, not only the crontab line.

blocks.question: An intruder with root wants code to run again after every reboot. Which of these places would a defender check? Pick the most complete answer.
options: Only /etc/crontab
Only /usr/lib/systemd/system, since admins never change /etc
/etc/systemd/system units and drop-ins, timers, system and user crontabs
/proc, because services are listed there
blocks.explain: Services, drop-ins and timers in /etc/systemd/system, and every crontab (system files and per-user tables), are all standard autostart places (ATT&CK T1543.002, T1053.003, T1053.006). /proc shows only what is running now.

blocks.question: What does `*/5 * * * *` in a crontab mean?
options: At 5 minutes past every hour
Every 5 hours
Every 5 minutes
On the 5th day of every month
blocks.explain: The first field is minutes; */5 means every value divisible by 5 within the range. All other fields are *, so the job runs every five minutes, every hour, every day.

lessons.title: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor

blocks.md:
Linux software is installed as **packages**: archives of files plus metadata (version, dependencies, checksums) managed by a package manager. Debian and Ubuntu use dpkg underneath APT (the Advanced Package Tool); Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux use RPM (the RPM Package Manager) underneath dnf. Packages come from repositories, servers that publish many packages with a signed index.

Updates are the single most effective defence on this list. Shellshock, PwnKit, Dirty COW and the SSH bug in lesson 10 were all fixed by installing a package update. The work is knowing what needs updating, applying it, and restarting whatever still runs the old code.

blocks.code:
# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update                 # fetch the signed package index
apt list --upgradable           # what would change
sudo apt upgrade                # install updates

# Fedora / RHEL
sudo dnf check-update
sudo dnf upgrade

# integrity: which package owns a file, and have its files changed?
dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd          # rpm -qf /usr/sbin/sshd on RPM systems
sudo dpkg --verify openssh-server   # rpm -V openssh-server
blocks.caption: Everyday update commands, then two integrity tools. dpkg --verify compares installed files against the checksums recorded when the package was installed; silence means no differences.

blocks.md:
How does APT know a package is genuine? `apt-secure(8)` describes the chain. A Debian maintainer signs each upload; once accepted, checksums of every package go into a `Packages` file, checksums of those go into a `Release` file, and the Release file is signed with the archive key. Your machine verifies that signature, then each checksum on the way down.

The same manual states the limit plainly: trusting an archive does not mean trusting its packages not to contain malicious code; it means you trust the archive maintainer. Signatures prove *who published* the software, not that the software is good. The next case shows exactly that gap.

**Case: the xz-utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094).** XZ Utils is a widely used compression library and tool, maintained for years by Lasse Collin. Russ Cox's timeline describes how a contributor using the name "Jia Tan" sent helpful patches from October 2021, while other accounts pressured the overworked maintainer to share control; Jia Tan became a co-maintainer and made releases from 2023. In February 2024 they added obfuscated binary data disguised as test files, and released versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 whose release tarballs (the downloadable source archives) contained an extra build script that was not in the public git repository.

When distributions built packages from those tarballs, the script spliced hidden code into `liblzma`. The OpenSSH server does not use liblzma directly, but Debian and several other distributions patch it to notify systemd, which pulls in `libsystemd`, which depends on liblzma. Through that chain the code ran inside `sshd` and hooked its key checking, creating a remote backdoor for whoever held the attacker's key.

blocks.title: How a compression library ended up inside the SSH server

scenes.caption: The public git repository looked normal. The extra build script (build-to-host.m4, a macro file for the m4 text processor used by build scripts) existed only in the release tarballs that maintainers download.
Distributions build from the tarball. At build time the script extracts code hidden in test files and links it into liblzma.
The package is signed and published normally. The signature is valid: it proves who published it, not what it contains.
On affected distributions sshd is patched to talk to systemd, so it loads libsystemd, which loads liblzma. The hidden code is now inside the SSH server.
Caught: Andres Freund, a software developer, noticed SSH logins using more CPU and running slower, plus errors from the memory checker valgrind, and traced them back to liblzma.

blocks.md: Andres Freund, a software developer who stressed in the report that they were not a security researcher, disclosed it to the oss-security mailing list (a public list for open-source security announcements) on 29 March 2024. Freund had seen odd symptoms on Debian unstable machines for weeks. Freund's measurements are the detection story: a failed SSH login to localhost took about 0.8 seconds instead of 0.3, and simply starting sshd with `-h` took about 0.5 seconds instead of 0.01 under the conditions the backdoor checked for. The code spent that time parsing symbol tables in memory to find what to hook.

scenes.caption: Failed SSH login to localhost, wall-clock time: about 0.3 s before, 0.8 s with the backdoored liblzma.
Running sshd -h with a clean environment: about 0.5 s when the backdoor activated, about 0.01 s when Freund set TERM so that it stayed dormant.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.** The backdoored versions reached mostly development and testing releases (Debian testing and unstable, Fedora Rawhide and the Fedora 40 beta) before discovery. CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) advised downgrading to an uncompromised version such as 5.4.6, hunting for malicious activity and reporting findings. Checking is a version question: `xz --version` or your package manager's query on every host.

The lessons for a Linux defender: keep an inventory of package versions so you can answer "are we affected?" in minutes; treat performance anomalies on security-critical daemons as worth a look; and know that a valid signature and a trusted repository do not rule out a malicious upstream. Running only stable releases bought time here, because the backdoor was caught before it reached them.

Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

blocks.question: A teammate argues: 'Our packages are signed by the distribution with GPG (GNU Privacy Guard, a signing tool), so a backdoored package is impossible.' What is the flaw?
options: A signature proves who published the package, not that the source they built from was free of malicious code
GPG signatures are easy to forge
Signatures only cover the package name
Signed packages are never verified by apt
blocks.explain: apt-secure(8) says so directly: trusting an archive means trusting its maintainer, not that packages are free of malicious code. The xz release tarballs were genuine releases by a project maintainer, and distribution packages built from them were validly signed.

blocks.question: What tipped off Andres Freund to the xz backdoor?
options: An antivirus alert
SSH logins using unusual CPU time and running slower, plus valgrind errors
A CVE published by the attacker
A failed package signature check
blocks.explain: No security tool flagged it. A developer noticed sshd taking about half a second longer and memory-checker errors, and refused to ignore the anomaly.

lessons.title: SSH: keys versus passwords, authorized_keys and hardening

blocks.md:
**SSH** (Secure Shell, defined in RFC 4251) is how almost everyone administers Linux servers: an encrypted remote login. Because it is exposed to the network and leads straight to a shell, it is a constant target: internet-facing SSH servers routinely receive automated password guesses.

SSH supports several ways to prove who you are (RFC 4252). The two that matter:

- **password**: you send your password through the encrypted channel and the server checks it against `/etc/shadow`. Guessable, reusable, and phishable.
- **publickey**: you hold a private key; the server holds the matching public key in your `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. You prove you hold the private key by signing data from this session. The private key never leaves your machine, so there is nothing to guess over the network and nothing reusable to steal from the server.

blocks.code:
# on your laptop: make a key pair (protect it with a passphrase)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice laptop"
# writes ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private, keep secret) and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public)

# install the public key on the server, then log in with it
ssh-copy-id alice@web1
ssh alice@web1

# on the server: one line per allowed key
cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIK... alice laptop
blocks.caption: Key setup end to end. Ed25519 is a modern signature algorithm with short keys (EdDSA, the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm, on Curve25519, named for the prime 2 to the 255 minus 19); the comment at the end of the line is only a label.

scenes.caption: The client connects. Encryption is set up first, so everything after this is protected from eavesdroppers.
The client says which user it wants and offers a public key.
sshd looks for that exact key in alice's authorized_keys, after checking the file is not writable by others (StrictModes).
The client signs data unique to this session with the private key. sshd verifies the signature with the public key. No secret crosses the network.
Accepted. sshd logs the method, user, source address and the key's fingerprint, so you can tell which key was used.

blocks.md:
The `authorized_keys` file is powerful and easy to overlook. Anyone who can append a line to it can log in as that user, with no password and no change to `/etc/shadow`. MITRE ATT&CK lists this as technique T1098.004, SSH Authorized Keys. The `sshd(8)` manual recommends that `~/.ssh` be accessible only by its owner and `authorized_keys` be readable and writable only by its owner, and sshd's `StrictModes` setting (on by default) refuses keys if those files or the home directory are writable by others.

Each key line can also carry restrictions in front of it, such as `from="203.0.113.0/24"` to accept the key only from addresses 203.0.113.0 to 203.0.113.255 (the /24 means the first 24 bits must match), or `restrict` for automation keys, which disables port forwarding (tunnelling other network connections through SSH), agent forwarding (letting the server use your loaded keys) and terminal allocation (an interactive shell).

The server's behaviour is set in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (`sshd_config(5)`). Defaults worth knowing: `PasswordAuthentication` is yes, `PermitRootLogin` is prohibit-password (root may log in with a key but not a password), `MaxAuthTries` is 6 attempts per connection, and `LoginGraceTime` is 120 seconds to finish logging in. A typical hardened configuration:

blocks.code:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf (low number: read first)
PasswordAuthentication no        # keys only: removes password guessing
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no  # close the other password-style route
PermitRootLogin no               # admins log in as themselves, then sudo
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowGroups ssh-users            # only members of this group may log in
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
X11Forwarding no                 # no remote graphical (X11) programs drawing on the client

# check the syntax, then reload without dropping current sessions
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(passwordauth|kbdinteractive|permitroot)'  # what is really in force
blocks.caption: sshd keeps the first value it reads for each keyword and reads drop-ins in name order, so an earlier file such as 50-cloud-init.conf can silently override yours. Name yours low and confirm with sshd -T. Keep a working session open while you reload.

blocks.md: Turning off password login does not help if an attacker can write to `authorized_keys`, and a private key copied from a laptop works from anywhere. Protect private keys with a passphrase, remove keys of people who leave, and review every `authorized_keys` file on your servers, including root's (`/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`).

Keys beat passwords because nothing guessable or reusable travels to the server. That moves the risk to the key files themselves: `authorized_keys` decides who gets in, so audit it like you audit sudoers.

blocks.question: After setting PasswordAuthentication no, which attack is still fully possible?
options: Online password guessing against sshd
Reading passwords off the network
Logging in to accounts with empty passwords
Logging in with a public key an intruder appended to a user's authorized_keys
blocks.explain: Disabling passwords stops guessing and empty-password logins. A key added to authorized_keys still authenticates normally, which is why that file is a favourite persistence spot.

blocks.question: sshd ignores alice's authorized_keys even though the key is correct. alice's home directory is mode 777. Why?
options: Ed25519 keys require mode 777
StrictModes refuses keys when the user's files or home directory are writable by others
The file must be owned by root
sshd only reads keys from /etc/ssh
blocks.explain: With a world-writable home directory any user could replace .ssh/authorized_keys. StrictModes (default yes) checks ownership and modes before trusting the file, so fix the permissions: home not writable by others, .ssh 700, authorized_keys 600.

lessons.title: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server

blocks.md:
Lesson 6 introduced signals: notifications that can interrupt a program at any instruction. That freedom has a cost. If a signal arrives while the program is halfway through updating a shared data structure, and the signal handler (the function that runs when the signal arrives) touches the same structure, the handler sees it half-updated. Functions that are safe to call from a handler are called **async-signal-safe**, and the list is short; `malloc` (memory allocation) and `syslog` (writing a log message) are not on it.

**Case: regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387).** The Qualys Threat Research Unit disclosed on 1 July 2024 that OpenSSH's server could be attacked through exactly this mistake, unauthenticated and as root, on Linux systems using glibc (the GNU C library).

The mechanism, from the Qualys advisory: if a client does not finish logging in within `LoginGraceTime` seconds (120 by default), sshd's `SIGALRM` handler (the alarm timer signal) runs and logs "Timeout before authentication". Logging calls `syslog()`, and glibc's `syslog()` can call `malloc()`. If the alarm interrupts sshd while it is in the middle of a `malloc()` of its own, the handler's `malloc()` works on a heap (the memory area malloc manages) left in an inconsistent state, and a carefully prepared inconsistency can be turned into code execution.

The name is the story. The researcher Mark Dowd had reported the same bug in 2006 (CVE-2006-5051) and it was fixed by making the handler skip the unsafe logging. In October 2020 a rework of OpenSSH's logging in version 8.5p1 accidentally removed that guard, so versions 8.5p1 to 9.7p1 (p1 marks the portable release for Linux and other systems) were vulnerable again: a **regression**, hence regreSSHion. OpenBSD's own system was not affected, because its handler uses `syslog_r()`, a safer variant OpenBSD added in 2001.

blocks.title: Why the alarm is dangerous only at one moment

scenes.caption: A normal client logs in within a few seconds. The alarm is cancelled and never fires.
A client that stalls: at 120 s the alarm fires while sshd is idle, waiting for data. The handler logs the timeout and exits. Unsafe, but harmless here.
The race: the attacker times its data so sshd is inside malloc (parsing a public key) exactly when the alarm fires at 120 s.
The handler's malloc runs on the half-updated heap. Winning takes around 10,000 attempts on average in Qualys's 32-bit tests, about 6 to 8 hours of connections per success.
Fixed in 9.8p1: the alarm handler no longer logs. The unsafe work moved to sshd's listener process, which handles it outside any signal handler.

blocks.caption: The fix works because _exit() is async-signal-safe: it ends the process without touching the heap, so an interrupted malloc can no longer be re-entered.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- Prevent: upgrade to OpenSSH 9.8p1 or your distribution's patched package. If you cannot, Qualys notes that `LoginGraceTime 0` removes the race at the cost of letting unauthenticated connections pile up (a denial-of-service risk).
- Reduce exposure: SSH does not need to face the whole internet. Restrict it with a firewall or VPN to the addresses that need it; then a remote, unauthenticated bug is reachable only from those addresses.
- Detect: the attack requires thousands of connections that never authenticate, so logs fill with "Timeout before authentication" lines from the same sources over hours. Recent OpenSSH versions also include per-source penalties (`PerSourcePenalties`, enabled by default) that throttle addresses behaving this way.

blocks.code:
ssh -V                               # client version on this machine
sshd -V                              # server version (OpenSSH 9.2 and later)
dpkg -l openssh-server               # or: rpm -q openssh-server

journalctl -u ssh --since today | grep -c 'Timeout before authentication'
blocks.caption: Version checks for an inventory, then a count of handshake timeouts today. A sudden jump in that count from a few addresses is the shape of this attack.

blocks.md: A signal handler can interrupt any line of code, so it must only do async-signal-safe work, and a fix must be guarded by a test or it can quietly disappear in a refactor, as this one did after 14 years.

blocks.question: Why was LoginGraceTime 0 an effective emergency mitigation for regreSSHion?
options: With no login time limit, the SIGALRM handler never fires, so there is no race to win
It disables password login
It makes sshd use syslog_r()
It blocks all unauthenticated connections
blocks.explain: The vulnerable code only runs when the grace-time alarm goes off. A value of 0 means no limit, so no alarm. The cost is that idle unauthenticated connections can exhaust MaxStartups (sshd's limit on connections still waiting to log in) and deny service.

blocks.question: What made this bug a 'regression'?
options: It only affected old 32-bit systems
It was introduced by the xz backdoor
A 2006 fix was accidentally removed during a 2020 logging rework, re-opening the same flaw
It regressed performance
blocks.explain: CVE-2006-5051 had been fixed by guarding the unsafe logging. Commit 752250c in OpenSSH 8.5p1 removed that guard while rewriting logging, so the old bug came back until 9.8p1.

lessons.title: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo

blocks.md:
A **log** is a timestamped record of events written by programs as they run. On a modern Linux system two layers are involved:

- **systemd-journald**, the journal daemon, collects messages from the kernel, services and programs into a structured, indexed store. You read it with `journalctl`.
- A **syslog** daemon, usually rsyslog (its project calls it the rocket-fast system for log processing), may also be installed; it receives the same messages and writes plain text files under `/var/log`.

Which text files exist depends on the distribution. Ubuntu's rsyslog configuration sends authentication messages to `/var/log/auth.log`; the Red Hat family's configuration sends them to `/var/log/secure`. Since Debian 12, rsyslog is no longer installed by default, so a fresh Debian server may have no `auth.log` at all: the journal is the source of truth.

The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

blocks.code:
journalctl -u ssh --since "2025-11-13 09:00"     # one service, from a time
journalctl -p warning -b                         # warnings and worse, this boot
journalctl -f                                    # follow new messages live
journalctl _COMM=sudo --since today              # everything the sudo program logged
sudo grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | tail   # text-file route, if rsyslog is present
blocks.caption: The journalctl options -u (unit), -p (priority), -b (boot), -f (follow) and field filters like _COMM cover most investigations.

blocks.md: Now the lines themselves. OpenSSH's `auth_log()` function builds every authentication message from one template: result, method, user, source address and port, and for keys the key type and fingerprint. That regularity is what makes these logs easy to search. Below is a short, invented sequence on server web1 showing the typical shape of a password-guessing attack that succeeds, followed by what the intruder did next.

blocks.code:
Nov 13 09:14:02 web1 sshd[2190]: Invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51522
Nov 13 09:14:04 web1 sshd[2190]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51522 ssh2
Nov 13 09:14:09 web1 sshd[2195]: Failed password for deploy from 203.0.113.45 port 51530 ssh2
Nov 13 09:14:15 web1 sshd[2198]: Failed password for deploy from 203.0.113.45 port 51544 ssh2
Nov 13 09:15:31 web1 sshd[2207]: Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.45 port 51602 ssh2
Nov 13 09:16:40 web1 sudo:   deploy : TTY=pts/1 ; PWD=/home/deploy ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/crontab -e
Nov 13 09:21:07 web1 sshd[2318]: Accepted publickey for alice from 198.51.100.7 port 50112 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:x1Fq...
blocks.caption: Invalid user means the name does not exist. Failed then Accepted for the same account from the same address is the line that matters. Note the different method: password for the attacker, publickey for alice. Since OpenSSH 9.8 the tag reads sshd-session[pid].

blocks.title: The same events on one timeline

scenes.caption: 09:14: guesses from 203.0.113.45 against a user that does not exist (admin) and a real one (deploy). Times are minutes after 09:10; blocks are widened so they are visible.
09:15:31: Accepted password for deploy from the same address. Failures followed by a success from one source is a classic detection rule.
09:16:40: one minute later deploy uses sudo to edit root's crontab. A new login followed quickly by privileged changes is escalation plus persistence.
09:21: alice logs in with alice's key from the usual address. Normal activity sits beside the attack; context (source, method, time) separates them.

blocks.md:
A few lines worth recognising beyond SSH:

- sudo denials (`user NOT in sudoers`, `command not allowed`, `3 incorrect password attempts`) show someone probing for privilege.
- `Timeout before authentication` in bulk points to scanners or, as in lesson 10, an attack on sshd itself.
- `last` lists past logins with source and duration from the wtmp login record, and `sudo lastb` lists failed ones (btmp); some newer distributions keep this in a wtmpdb database, read with the same `last` command.
- PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules, the library layer most login programs use to check passwords) logs lines containing `authentication failure` with the user and source.
- Gaps in time, or logs that stop abruptly, matter too: clearing logs is a known intruder step (ATT&CK T1685.006). Sending logs to a separate machine as they are written means an intruder with root cannot erase what already left the box.

blocks.code:
# top source addresses of failed SSH passwords today
journalctl -u ssh --since today | grep 'Failed password' \
  | grep -oE 'from [0-9a-f.:]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# successful logins, with method and source
journalctl -u ssh --since today | grep 'Accepted'
blocks.caption: Two everyday triage pipelines. The first counts failures per source address; the second lists every successful login so you can check each one is expected.

blocks.md: Learn the shape of four lines: Failed password, Accepted (password or publickey), sudo COMMAND, and sudo denials. Then look for sequences, not single lines: failures then success from one source, and a fresh login followed by privileged changes.

blocks.question: Your Debian 12 server has no /var/log/auth.log. What is the most likely explanation?
options: SSH logging is disabled by default
An attacker deleted it
auth.log was renamed to secure
rsyslog is no longer installed by default, so authentication messages are only in the systemd journal
blocks.explain: Debian 12 release notes: rsyslog is no longer installed by default. Messages go to the journal; read them with journalctl -u ssh. An attacker is possible, but check the simple explanation first. /var/log/secure is the Red Hat name.

blocks.question: Which log sequence most strongly suggests a successful password-guessing attack?
options: Many Invalid user lines from many addresses, no Accepted lines
Several Failed password for deploy from one address, then Accepted password for deploy from the same address
Accepted publickey for alice from alice's usual address
One sudo line for alice restarting nginx
blocks.explain: Background scanning (many invalid users, no success) is routine. Repeated failures for a real account followed by success from the same source means a guess worked. Treat the account as compromised.

lessons.title: What an intruder touches: persistence and where defenders look

blocks.md: After getting in, an intruder usually wants three things: higher privilege, a way back in that survives reboots and password changes (**persistence**), and fewer traces. Every one of those goals requires changing something on the system, and the places are few and well known. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues them; this lesson maps each one to the defender's check. The point is not to learn the techniques but to know where evidence appears.

blocks.title: Persistence locations on a Linux host

scenes.caption: The host, with the places earlier lessons covered. Each is a way to run code or log in again later.
Way back in: a key appended to some authorized_keys (T1098.004), or a new account, possibly with UID 0 (T1136.001).
Code that reruns: cron entries (T1053.003), systemd services and timers (T1543.002, T1053.006), and shell startup files like ~/.bashrc (T1546.004).
Privilege for later: a copied shell or other program with the setuid bit, owned by root (T1548.001).
Tools and traces: binaries dropped in world-writable /tmp, and edited or cleared logs (T1070.002).
The defender's version: every one of these is a file with an owner and a modification time, so a baseline and a diff catch most of them.

blocks.md: Shell startup files deserve a sentence of explanation. When bash starts as a login shell it runs `/etc/profile` and then the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` or `~/.profile` it finds; interactive shells that are not login shells run `~/.bashrc` (many distributions' `~/.profile` also runs it for login shells). A line added there runs every time that user logs in or opens a terminal, which ATT&CK lists as T1546.004. Admins rarely reread these files, which is exactly why they are used.

blocks.code:
# accounts: UID 0 entries and recently changed account files
grep -E '^[^:]*:[^:]*:0:' /etc/passwd
ls -l --time-style=long-iso /etc/passwd /etc/shadow /etc/group /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d

# keys: every authorized_keys file, newest first
getent passwd | cut -d: -f6 | sort -u | while read -r h; do
  sudo find "$h/.ssh" -maxdepth 1 -name 'authorized_keys*' -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM %u %p\n' 2>/dev/null
done | sort -r

# scheduled code: crontabs, systemd units and timers changed in the last 7 days
sudo ls -la /etc/cron.d /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null
sudo find /etc/systemd/system /etc/cron* -mtime -7 -type f
systemctl list-timers --all
sudo ls -la /home/*/.config/systemd/user 2>/dev/null   # per-user units
ls -l /etc/ld.so.preload 2>/dev/null                   # normally absent

# privilege: setuid files compared with a saved baseline
sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 | sort | sudo diff /root/suid-baseline.txt -

# running code: processes whose program file was deleted
sudo ls -l /proc/*/exe 2>/dev/null | grep '(deleted)'
blocks.caption: A first-response sweep that only reads. Where per-user crontabs are stored under /var/spool/cron varies by distribution.

blocks.md:
Two habits make this sweep far more effective. First, take baselines while the system is known good: lists of accounts, keys, units, setuid files and package versions. Without a baseline, "is this normal?" is guesswork. Second, prefer evidence the intruder cannot easily edit: logs already shipped to another server, and file checksums kept off the host or checked from trusted boot media, for example with AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment). Package verification (`dpkg --verify`, `rpm -V`) is a quick first look, but it trusts a local database that root can rewrite. Tools such as **Lynis**, an open-source security auditing tool from the company CISOfy, which checks a host against a long list of hardening and integrity items.

Finally, if you find one persistence mechanism, assume there are others. Intruders commonly install more than one way back in; removing the first you find and declaring victory is how incidents recur. For a confirmed root compromise, the reliable fix is to rebuild the host from known-good sources and rotate every credential it held.

Do not investigate a live compromise only with the compromised system's own tools if you can avoid it: an intruder with root can alter `ps`, `ls` or the logs. Cross-check with package verification, a trusted copy of the tools, or off-host data.

blocks.question: During a sweep you find an unfamiliar key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys added last night. You remove it. Why is the incident not over?
options: Whoever added it had root, and may also have left cron jobs, units, accounts or setuid files
Removing keys never takes effect until reboot
Keys in /root are ignored by sshd anyway
The key will regenerate itself
blocks.explain: Writing to /root/.ssh requires root. An intruder with root rarely leaves only one way back, so check every persistence location, find how they got in, and for a confirmed root compromise plan a rebuild and credential rotation.

blocks.question: Which check would catch an intruder who copied /bin/bash to /var/tmp/.x and set the setuid bit (owner root)?
options: Listing /etc/systemd/system
A setuid file search compared with a baseline
journalctl -u ssh
Checking /etc/passwd for UID 0
blocks.explain: The new file is a root-owned setuid program that gives a root shell on demand. A find -perm -4000 diffed against a baseline shows a new setuid file, provided the search covers every mounted filesystem (-xdev stops at mount points, so run it per mount).

lessons.title: A basic hardening checklist and where to practise

blocks.md: **Hardening** means reducing what an attacker can reach and what they can do once there. It is not one setting but a set of habits, each closing a door this course opened. Here is the course as a checklist, ordered roughly by how much risk each step removes for the effort.

1. **Patch.** Enable automatic security updates where you can, and reboot for kernel and core library updates. Every case in this course was fixed by an update.
2. **Expose less.** Run only the services you need (`systemctl list-units --type=service`), and limit SSH to the networks that need it.
3. **SSH keys only.** `PasswordAuthentication no`, `PermitRootLogin no`, an `AllowGroups` list, and reviewed `authorized_keys` files.
4. **Least privilege.** Named accounts, sudo rules for specific commands, no `NOPASSWD: ALL`, services running as their own unprivileged users with systemd sandboxing options.
5. **Permissions.** No world-writable files run by root, sensible umask, a setuid baseline, `nosuid` on mounts that do not need it such as `/tmp` where your distribution allows.
6. **Logs that survive.** Persistent journal, logs shipped off the host, and someone or something that reads them.
7. **Baselines.** Accounts, keys, units, crontabs, setuid files and package versions, recorded while known good.

blocks.title: Which checklist item would have stopped each case

scenes.caption: Patching fixes all five cases in this course once an update exists. 1 means the step fully blocks the case, 0.5 that it limits damage or exposure, 0 that it does not help.
Exposing SSH only to trusted networks: regreSSHion and the xz backdoor needed network access to sshd, so restricting it shrinks who can try. It does nothing for local bugs.
Removing unneeded setuid bits: PwnKit is harmless without pkexec's setuid bit, which is exactly Qualys's mitigation. The others are unaffected.
Not running shell CGI scripts would have removed the main remote route for Shellshock on web servers.

blocks.md: Notice what the chart says: no single control covers everything, and patching is the only one that helps in every case, but only after a fix exists. The xz backdoor had no patch until it was found, and Dirty COW was exploited in the wild before disclosure. That is why layers matter: exposure limits, least privilege and logs reduce damage during the window before a fix, and baselines tell you afterwards whether the window was used.

blocks.code:
# a ten-minute audit of a host you are responsible for
uname -r; cat /etc/os-release | head -2       # kernel and distribution versions
apt list --upgradable 2>/dev/null | head      # or: dnf check-update
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin|allowgroups)'
sudo -l -U deploy                             # what a service account may do
grep -E '^[^:]*:[^:]*:0:' /etc/passwd
sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 | wc -l
ls -ld /var/log/journal                       # persistent journal present?
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
sudo ss -tulpn                                 # what listens on which port, and which program
sudo lynis audit system                       # if Lynis is installed
blocks.caption: sshd -T prints the effective configuration after all includes, which is more reliable than reading the file. Lynis prints findings and suggestions with test IDs.

blocks.md: Practise on systems you own or on platforms built for it, never on machines you do not have written permission to test. In this course everything happens on your own host, which is the right place to start.

**Where to practise legally.**

- [OverTheWire Bandit](https://overthewire.org/wargames/bandit/): a wargame aimed at absolute beginners, played over SSH. Each level is a small puzzle about files, permissions, processes and tools covered here.
- [pwn.college Linux Luminarium](https://pwn.college/linux-luminarium/): free hands-on modules from a team at Arizona State University, including users, permissions, processes and PATH.
- Your own virtual machine: install a Debian or Ubuntu server, apply this checklist, run Lynis before and after, and read your own `journalctl -u ssh` output for a day after exposing SSH.

Patch, expose less, use keys, grant little, keep logs off the box and keep baselines. Each step is simple; together they turn most of the attacks in this course from silent root into a noisy, short-lived event.

blocks.question: Which control helps against the most cases in this course, and what is its blind spot?
options: Disabling password SSH; it does nothing for local bugs
Removing setuid bits; it breaks passwd
Patching; it cannot help before a fix exists, as with the xz backdoor before discovery
Log shipping; it prevents nothing
blocks.explain: Every case was fixed by an update, but updates arrive only after someone finds the bug. That window is why exposure limits, least privilege, logs and baselines are layered on top.

blocks.question: You can make one change today on an internet-facing server that still allows SSH passwords and has 30 user accounts. Which change removes the most risk?
options: Set PasswordAuthentication no after giving every user a key
Change the SSH port
Delete /var/log/auth.log to save space
Set umask 000
blocks.explain: Thirty passwords means thirty chances that one is weak or reused, and guessing is constant on the internet. Keys remove online guessing entirely. A different port only reduces noise; deleting logs and umask 000 make things worse.
